title: Concerto for Orchestra
hook: Written by an exile, ill and nearly silent, it moves from a grave night to a whirling dance.

painting.title: The Solitary Cedar
painting.pairingNote: A lone tree on a far shore, by a Hungarian painter little understood in his lifetime; Bartók wrote the concerto alone and ill, far from Hungary.

facts: In October 1940 Bartók left Hungary, then drawing closer to Nazi Germany, and settled in New York with his wife, the pianist Ditta Pásztory. America was hard for him: little money, few concerts, and from 1943 an illness that was later identified as leukaemia. He had almost stopped composing.

Two Hungarian musicians in America, the violinist Joseph Szigeti and the conductor Fritz Reiner, asked Serge Koussevitzky of the Boston Symphony Orchestra to help. In 1943 Koussevitzky visited Bartók in hospital and offered him $1,000 for an orchestral work in memory of his wife, Natalie.

Bartók wrote it in about eight weeks, from 15 August to 8 October 1943, at a health resort at Saranac Lake in upstate New York. Koussevitzky conducted the premiere in Boston on 1 December 1944 and, Bartók reported, called it the best orchestral piece of the last 25 years. In February 1945 Bartók wrote a new ending for the finale.

Why “concerto”? In his own note Bartók said the work treats single instruments or groups “in a concertant or soloistic manner”. Every section of the orchestra gets its turn in the spotlight. He also described its course: from the sternness of the first movement and the “lugubrious death-song” of the third to the life-affirming finale.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dark introduction and a fierce allegro (I), a game of pairs (II), a night lament at the centre (III), a song interrupted by a parody (IV), a whirling dance that ends in triumph (V). The five movements mirror each other around the third.

movements.heading: Introduzione
movements.title: Introduzione
movements.summary: A slow, mysterious introduction grows out of a theme rising in fourths in the low strings. It speeds up into a fierce, fast movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]]: a leaping main theme, a bold call on the trombone and a gentle, folk-like tune on the oboe. In the middle the brass build the trombone’s call into a [[fugato|fugato]].

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: a slow, hushed line for cellos and basses that climbs in wide steps (fourths), answered by shimmering upper strings.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a fast, springing tune in the violins, also built on leaps of a fourth.

mainIdeas.name: The trombone call
mainIdeas.description: a short, bold fanfare, again made of fourths.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: a quiet oboe tune that rocks back and forth like a folk song.

stops.hear: Cellos and basses, very quietly, climb in wide steps; high strings answer with a soft shimmer; flutes join
Trumpets play a quiet, solemn phrase
stops.happening: A first glimpse of the brass

stops.hear: The strings grow restless and the music speeds up
stops.happening: The approach to the fast music

stops.hear: The violins leap in with a fast, springing theme
A solo trombone sounds a short, bold call
The music calms; the oboe sings a gentle tune, rocking between a few notes over a soft background
stops.happening: The second theme, close to a folk song

stops.hear: Fragments of the themes are tossed around the orchestra
The brass enter one after another with the trombone’s call and pile it up
The quiet tunes return first
The springing main theme comes back

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The brass blaze out the fanfare once more; the movement stops short

notice: Listen for the interval of a fourth: in the slow opening, in the main theme and in the trombone call. One small shape holds the movement together.
In the brass fugato, count the entries: each player begins the same call a little after the previous one.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Fritz Reiner had known Bartók since 1905 and was reportedly one of the two musicians who asked Koussevitzky to commission this work. He made its first recording in 1946 with the Pittsburgh Symphony; this one, with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, followed in October 1955. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 1–5.

movements.heading: Giuoco delle coppie
movements.title: Giuoco delle coppie
movements.summary: “The game of pairs.” A side drum taps out a rhythm alone. Then five pairs of wind instruments take turns, each pair playing in parallel at its own fixed distance: bassoons, oboes, clarinets, flutes, then [[muted|muted]] trumpets. A solemn brass [[chorale|chorale]] stands in the middle, and then the pairs come back, more richly accompanied.

mainIdeas.name: The side drum
mainIdeas.description: a dry rhythm that opens and closes the movement.

mainIdeas.name: The pairs
mainIdeas.description: each pair plays its own short, dancing tune, always moving together at the same interval.

mainIdeas.name: The chorale
mainIdeas.description: a slow hymn for the brass.

stops.hear: A side drum alone, tapping a dry rhythm
Two bassoons play a jaunty tune side by side
Two oboes, closer together, brighter
Two clarinets, with a sharper, more sour sound
Two flutes, light and hollow
Two muted trumpets, rubbing against each other
stops.happening: Pair 5: trumpets, only a second apart

stops.hear: Slow, solemn chords in the brass
The bassoons start again; this time a third bassoon joins in with a line of its own

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: The side drum, alone again

notice: Listen to the distance between the two instruments of each pair. Sixths and thirds sound sweet; sevenths and seconds sound tart.
The side drum both opens and closes the movement, like a frame around a picture.

movements.heading: Elegia
movements.title: Elegia
movements.summary: The heart of the work, and what Bartók called its death-song. Mysterious ripples in the woodwind and harp surround slow, grieving melodies taken from the first movement. It is an example of Bartók’s [[night-music|night music]]: soft, strange sounds like the noises of a night outdoors.

mainIdeas.name: The night sounds
mainIdeas.description: rippling woodwind, harp and quiet string figures.

mainIdeas.name: The laments
mainIdeas.description: broad, passionate melodies in the strings, drawn from the slow opening of the first movement.

stops.hear: Low strings, dark and hushed, recall the work’s opening
Rippling flutes and clarinets, harp, and a lonely oboe line
The strings break out in a passionate, crying melody
The music swells to a loud climax, then sinks back
Violas, then the strings, sing another broad melody
Another anguished climax for the whole orchestra

stops.label: Last 1:15
stops.hear: The rippling night sounds return, and the movement fades
stops.happening: The night music closes the movement

notice: Listen to the background as much as the melody. The ripples and murmurs in woodwind and harp are the “night” around the lament.
The laments do not come from nowhere. They grow out of the slow opening of the whole concerto.

movements.heading: Intermezzo interrotto
movements.title: Intermezzo interrotto
movements.summary: “Interrupted intermezzo.” A quirky oboe tune alternates with a warm, nostalgic melody in the violas. Then a vulgar, jaunty tune breaks in and is mocked with jeering trills and sliding trombones. It is widely heard as a parody of a march from Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony, then famous in America; the tune also recalls Lehár’s operetta *The Merry Widow*. Afterwards the nostalgic melody returns.

mainIdeas.name: The oboe tune
mainIdeas.description: lively and off-balance, its metre keeps changing.

mainIdeas.name: The viola melody
mainIdeas.description: broad and tender, based on a Hungarian song in praise of the homeland.

mainIdeas.name: The interruption
mainIdeas.description: a cheap, catchy tune, laughed at by the orchestra.

stops.hear: The oboe plays a skipping tune with an uneven step
The violas sing a warm, broad melody
The violins take up the melody
The skipping oboe tune returns
Suddenly a clarinet plays a jaunty, vulgar tune over an oom-pah accompaniment
The woodwind cackle with trills; trombones and tuba slide rudely downwards
The strings play a distorted version of the tune
The warm melody returns, softer

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Scraps of the oboe tune; the movement ends quietly

notice: Listen for the laughter: fast trills in the woodwind and sliding notes in the brass.
Compare the warm viola melody with the tune that interrupts it. One sounds like a memory of home, the other like a street song.

movements.heading: Finale
movements.title: Finale
movements.summary: After a call on the horns, the strings set off in a whirling [[perpetuum-mobile|perpetuum mobile]] of village dance rhythms. A trumpet tune becomes the subject of a large fugue, and after a quiet, mysterious passage the dance returns. The movement ends with the brass in triumph and a final rush upwards: the “life-assertion” Bartók wrote of.

mainIdeas.name: The whirl
mainIdeas.description: fast, unbroken running notes in the strings, like a frantic folk dance.

mainIdeas.name: The trumpet tune
mainIdeas.description: a bright melody that becomes a fugue subject.

stops.hear: Horns play a short, heavy call
The strings start a whirling run of fast notes that hardly stops
Stamping dance rhythms, with the whole orchestra joining in
Trumpets play a bright, strutting tune
The tune is passed from instrument to instrument, piling up voice on voice
The music becomes quiet and mysterious, with soft rustling figures
The whirling strings return
The brass proclaim the trumpet tune, slow and grand, over the racing orchestra

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A final rush and a brilliant close

notice: Follow the strings at the start. They play almost without a break for minutes on end.
Compare the end with the first movement’s opening. The concerto began in darkness, with low strings alone; it ends in full light, with the whole orchestra.

threads.title: From night to day
threads.body: Bartók himself described the plan: from the sternness of the first movement through the death-song of the third to the life-affirming finale.

threads.title: A mirror
threads.body: The five movements are arranged symmetrically: two large outer movements, two lighter scherzo-like movements, and the Elegia at the centre.

threads.title: Everyone a soloist
threads.body: Each section has its moment: the brass in the fugato, the wind pairs in the second movement, the violas with the Hungarian song, the strings in the finale’s whirl.

threads.title: Hungary far away
threads.body: Folk-like tunes and dance rhythms run through the work, written in America by a composer who had spent decades collecting the music of Hungarian villages.
